newsitem.title: CHINA: Britain raises HK rights "threat" in report to UN.
newsitem.headline: Britain raises HK rights "threat" in report to UN.

text.p: Britain has told the United Nations about perceived threats to democracy and human rights in its ex-colony Hong Kong, now a special region of China.
Britain highlighted a number of concerns, including the establishment of an unelected legislature, in its final human rights report on Hong Kong to the U.N. Human Rights Committee in Geneva.
"The United Kingdom Government has never accepted that there was any need for a Provisional Legislature," said the report, made available to media in Hong Kong on Friday.

"It has called upon the Chinese Government...to ensure that the (new Hong Hong government) takes steps as soon as possible after the handover to replace the Provisional Legislature with a substantive legislature constituted by genuine election," the 27-page report said.

Beijing disbanded the elected Legislative Council when it took over the territory on July 1 and replaced it with a 60-member unelected interim assembly, chosen by a 400-strong China-controlled committee, pending elections due in a year.

The report also expressed concern about China's plan to repeal six liberal Hong Kong laws on political liberties, which were passed in the early 1990s in conformity with the territory's Bill of Rights.

The Bill of Rights, based on the International Convenant on Civil and Political Rights, provides statutory protection to Hong Kong's 6.4 million people after the bloody 1989 crackdown on a student-led democracy movement in Beijing.
The Provisional Legislature has approved a rollback of two of the six laws, narrowing political liberties and civil rights.
"The Ordinances ... are entirely consistent with the Covenant and, it follows, with the Basic Law," the report said.
The Basic Law is Hong Kong's new constitution.
"The United Kingdom Government accordingly sees no justification for undoing or replacing the original amendments," it said.

The British government pledged it would continue to monitor and report on developments in Hong Kong and on the implementation of the Sino-British handover treaty, the Joint Declaration, through regular reports to parliament.
Britain handed Hong Kong back to China at midnight on Monday, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
China, which is not a signatory to the international covenant, has so far declined to submit human rights report to the U.N. Human Rights Commission on behalf of Hong Kong.
